summary: DNS NOTIFY (RFC 1996) was designed to nudge servers to fetch zone updates. This document generalizes it so a notification can trigger other predefined actions. The notification only prompts the receiver to act sooner than its schedule; it does not carry the data itself.

plainLanguage.summary: A doorbell does not hand you a package; it just tells you to come get it. This lets DNS servers ring the doorbell for more kinds of jobs than just zone copying.

questions: how does generalized dns notify work
subtitle: Extends DNS NOTIFY beyond zone transfers so a child zone can nudge its parent to check for new DS or NS data right away.

tldr.problem: Parents scan child zones for new CDS, CDNSKEY and CSYNC records. Scanning many delegations is either costly when frequent or slow to converge when infrequent.
tldr.mechanism: A parent publishes a new DSYNC record under a _dsync name saying where to send NOTIFY messages. The child sends NOTIFY(CDS) or NOTIFY(CSYNC) there, and the receiver schedules an immediate check.
tldr.outcome: Updates reach the parent sooner. A notification only changes timing, so the usual security checks still apply, and receivers MUST rate limit.

today: RFC 9859 is a Proposed Standard published in September 2025. It is not obsoleted by or updated by any other RFC in the unit metadata.

sections.title: Why Generalize NOTIFY
sections.content:
The original DNS NOTIFY (RFC 1996), here called NOTIFY(SOA), lets a primary server tell a secondary server that a zone changed, which cuts convergence time. Today similar inefficiencies appear in delegation maintenance, meaning updates to DS and NS records.

This document lets other kinds of NOTIFY act as triggers. A notification only nudges the receiver to start a predefined action promptly instead of on a schedule; it does not change the action or its security checks. No DNS protocol changes are introduced: the mechanism uses a wider range of messages the protocol already allows. Its main application is delegation maintenance, and uses such as multi-signer key exchange are left for future work.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of checking the mailbox every hour, you get a short knock when something arrives, then you check it the usual way.

sections.title: The Scanning Problem
sections.content:
With RFC 1996, a pull mechanism (periodic SOA queries, paced by the SOA Refresh parameter) was supplemented with a push (NOTIFY) for a case that was otherwise inefficient.

CDS and CSYNC scanners are deployed in a growing number of TLD registries. Because of the many child delegations, scanning is slow, meaning infrequent. Few delegations will have changed between scan runs, yet frequent scanning is costly and infrequent scanning delays the DS update. Unlike the SOA case, there is no mechanism like SOA Refresh for the child to suggest a scanning interval. The same holds for NS and glue maintenance via CSYNC (RFC 7477).
sections.plainLanguage: Checking every house in a huge town for news is slow or wasteful. A knock from the one house with news is much better.

sections.title: The DSYNC Record
sections.content:
The new DSYNC record type tells senders where to deliver notifications. Its wire format has four fields:

  • RRtype: the type of generalized NOTIFY. For now only CDS and CSYNC are supported, CDS standing for an updated CDS or CDNSKEY set.
  • Scheme: an 8-bit unsigned integer giving the contact mode. 0 (null scheme) is ignored, 1 is defined here, and 128-255 are Reserved for Private Use.
  • Port: a 16-bit unsigned integer in network byte order. A value of 0 is ignored.
  • Target: a fully-qualified, uncompressed domain name that MUST resolve to one or more address records.

Scheme 1 has the mnemonic NOTIFY. Publishing it means the parent wants a NOTIFY message, over conventional DNS transport, when a new CDS/CDNSKEY/CSYNC RRset is published. Schemes are independent of the RRtype: they define how to contact the target, while the RRtype is part of the payload.
sections.plainLanguage: The record is like a sign on the door of the post office saying which window to knock on, and for which kind of news.

sections.title: Publishing Notification Targets
sections.content:
Parents that take part MUST publish DSYNC records under the _dsync subdomain of the parent zone. There MUST NOT be more than one DSYNC record per combination of RRtype and Scheme, and signing the zone with DNSSEC is RECOMMENDED. The parent MAY delegate _dsync as a separate zone or synthesize records under it.

Two publication styles exist:

  • Wildcard: a default target such as *._dsync.example. IN DSYNC CDS NOTIFY port target, useful when the parent processes the records itself or relays them. Dropping the wildcard label and publishing at _dsync is NOT RECOMMENDED because discovery needs an extra step.
  • Child-specific: the parent's labels are stripped from the child name and used instead of the wildcard, for example child._dsync.example. IN DSYNC CDS NOTIFY 5300 rr-endpoint.example. where a registrar provides the endpoint.
sections.plainLanguage: A town can put up one sign for everyone, or a separate sign pointing each family to a different window.

sections.title: Discovery and Sending
sections.content:
NOTIFY messages for delegation maintenance MUST be formatted as in RFC 1996 with the qtype replaced. NOTIFY(CDS) signals child-side changes to an upcoming DS update, and NOTIFY(CSYNC) does the same for CSYNC.

To find the target, the sender MUST insert the _dsync label after the first label of the delegation name, query DSYNC (validating if DNSSEC is enabled), and on a negative answer either insert the label just before the parent zone labels indicated by the SOA, or drop labels in front of _dsync, or give up with no target.

When it creates or changes a CDS/CDNSKEY/CSYNC RRset, the child DNS operator SHOULD notify one discovered endpoint. One NOTIFY can concern only one child zone, so several zones need separate messages. Because publication can take time to reach all copies, the child is RECOMMENDED to delay the NOTIFY until a consistent public view exists.
sections.plainLanguage: The child follows a short set of steps to find the right door, knocks about one house at a time, and waits until the news is really out before knocking.

sections.title: Receiving, Errors and Reports
sections.content:
A receiver discards any NOTIFY carrying records for more than one child zone. Otherwise it has two options. It can acknowledge with a NOTIFY response and schedule an immediate check of the child's CDS/CDNSKEY/CSYNC RRsets. Or it can ignore the notification, preferably still acknowledging so the sender does not retry; a rate limit is one reason, and the extended DNS error "Blocked" (15) may fit.

If a scanner is in use, a confirmed NOTIFY-driven change may lower that child's scanning frequency (for example to once a week). A change later found by scanning alone SHOULD clear that state. Senders without a response SHOULD act as for SOA notifications in RFC 1996.

Since processing can fail after the response, senders MAY add an EDNS0 Report-Channel option (RFC 9567) so errors come back as a report query with an extended DNS error code (RFC 8914). The agent domain MUST be subordinate or equal to one of the NS hostnames in the child's delegation, so that senders cannot aim reports at unrelated third parties.
sections.plainLanguage: The parent says thanks for the knock and goes to check, or politely says it is too busy. If something goes wrong, the child can ask to be told.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
A notification affects only the timing of an action, so the action runs under the same security model as if something else had triggered it. DS bootstrapping, for instance, keeps all its authentication requirements. Because of this, the sender's identity is not crucial and securing notifications is not required.

Receivers MUST implement rate limiting, and it is RECOMMENDED to configure it independently for the source IP address and the zone name in the NOTIFY. This also bounds the cost of garbage notifications and the extra work when outgoing queries use encrypted transport. Signing notifications appears significantly more expensive without tangible benefit.

Zones with DSYNC records are not required to be signed. Spoofed answers could stop notifications from reaching the real target or send them to another party, who could then learn their contents in real time, a possible privacy concern. A sender may choose to ignore unsigned DSYNC records.
sections.plainLanguage: The doorbell only says come look, so a prankster who rings it cannot change what you find. You just limit how often you answer.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content:
IANA registered the DSYNC RR type with value 66, meaning endpoint discovery for delegation synchronization. It also created a registry named "DSYNC: Location of Synchronization Endpoints" with Expert Review as its registration procedure, and registered the _dsync underscore name for DSYNC.

The initial registry has scheme 0 (null), scheme 1 (NOTIFY) for both CDS and CSYNC, scheme 2-127 unassigned and 128-255 for private use. Reviewers should discourage point squatting and may allow early assignment before a specification exists.
sections.plainLanguage: A public list of numbers was started so everyone agrees what each number means.

fields.name: RRtype
fields.desc: Type of generalized NOTIFY; CDS or CSYNC for now.

fields.name: Scheme
fields.desc: Contact mode; 1 is NOTIFY, 0 is ignored.

fields.name: Port
fields.desc: Transport port of the notification service; 0 is ignored.
